title: Coalescer timer drift micro-freezes and request-size skew retrospective
creator: Aisha Kapoor
description: Summary: A sequence of short, periodic micro-freezes in the continuous coalescer caused repeated short tail-latency spikes across multiple serving clusters. The symptom set looked like transient 50-500ms pauses that correlated with elevated tail latency on small, high-QPS requests. This ticket captures the incident timeline, root-cause analysis, temporary mitigations we rolled out, and concrete action items to prevent recurrence.
incident_summary: On 2026-02-14 between 18:12 and 19:05 UTC we observed recurring 50-500ms lat spikes in the continuous batcher across 3 regions. The spikes occurred in short pulses every ~7-12 minutes and disproportionately affected small synchronous text-generation requests. Throughput and error rates remained normal; the primary impact was degraded P95/P99 latency causing client timeouts for low-latency slices.
timeline: 2026-02-14T18:12:00Z - First alert: P95 for single-turn small requests exceeded SLO in eu-west-1
2026-02-14T18:18:00Z - Alerts from us-east-1 and ap-southeast-1 showing the same pulse pattern
2026-02-14T18:25:00Z - On-call engaged; initial hypothesis: backend kernel scheduling or GC
2026-02-14T18:36:00Z - Deployed extra debug metrics for coalescer wake / sleep events and per-request wait time histograms
2026-02-14T18:50:00Z - Observed coalescer wake events aligning across pods and a tight cluster of 6-8ms busy-wait followed by 100-400ms blocked intervals
2026-02-14T19:00:00Z - Hotfix v1 deployed: switch coalescer clock source to monotonic_raw where available and add small randomized jitter to wake timers
2026-02-14T19:08:00Z - Latency pulse frequency dropped and P99 returned near baseline; monitoring remained for 2 hours
2026-02-15T09:00:00Z - Full RCA kickoff: deeper trace analysis and code review of batching scheduler and size-prioritization logic

2026-02-18T11:30:00Z - Identified second contributing factor: size-aware prioritizer had an edge-case where a promotion threshold drifted, leading to sustained tiny-request favoritism under specific queuing patterns
2026-02-19T15:00:00Z - Hotfix v2 deployed: clamp promotion thresholds and add fairness window to prevent starvation of medium-size requests
2026-02-20T12:00:00Z - Documented final remediation and action items; ticket created for follow-ups
root_cause: Primary cause: coalescer relied on a wall-clock-derived timer on some platforms which experienced micro-jitter due to interplay with host-level NTP/clocksource switching and container pause semantics. These micro-jitter events synchronized across pods (common base AMI and startup timing), producing repeated brief pauses in batch formation. Secondary cause: size-aware prioritization used an adaptive promotion threshold that could drift toward over-prioritizing tiny requests when queue shapes changed rapidly, amplifying unfairness during pulses.
mitigation: Immediate mitigations: (1) switched coalescer timer to a monotonic_raw clock where supported; (2) introduced small randomized jitter to wake timers to break synchronization; (3) rolled a config flag to cap tiny-request priority promotion. Medium-term mitigations include adding per-pod jitter at startup, increasing observability around clocksource/ntp events, and adding a canary job that simulates steady tiny-request load to validate fairness.
action_items: ENG-33110 - Replace all uses of wall-clock timers in coalescer with steady monotonic APIs where available (owner: Tomás Nguyen, due: 2026-02-28)
ENG-33111 - Add startup jitter and periodic jitter to coalescer wake timers to avoid cross-pod synchronization (owner: Priya Shah, due: 2026-03-05)
ENG-33112 - Implement a fairness window in the prioritizer to prevent sustained tiny-request domination (owner: Marcus Lee, due: 2026-03-12)
ENG-33113 - Add telemetry: per-pod coalescer sleep/wake histogram, timer-source metric, and queuing shape heatmaps to runtime-telemetry dashboard (owner: Aisha Kapoor, due: 2026-03-01)
ENG-33114 - Create a load-canary job that reproduces tiny-request high-QPS traffic to detect skew regressions in pre-prod (owner: Signe Eriksson, due: 2026-03-08)
ENG-33115 - Run an infra audit of base AMI/kernel versions across clusters and document clocksource differences that could affect timers (owner: DevOps Team, due: 2026-03-10)
ENG-33116 - Postmortem write-up and customer communication review; prepare templated explanation for impacted customers and internal ops runbook update (owner: Tomás Nguyen, due: 2026-02-25)
postmortem_notes: We considered but rejected a coarse-grained batching timeout increase because it would raise average latency for many customers. The jitter approach preserves latency SLOs while breaking harmful synchronization. Also found that small-request prioritization remains valuable for PLG UX but must be bounded and observable.
retrospective: Key learning: highly-optimized runtime components that are deployed homogeneously can fail in lockstep due to subtle platform interactions (clocksource, container pause). Observability needs to include host-level signals and the scheduler must assume adversarial alignment. Moving forward we will treat timer-source and startup timing as first-class invariants in testing and canarying.
notes_for_oncall: If similar pulses reoccur: (1) toggle coalescer.jitter to non-zero to break sync; (2) enable tiny-priority-cap config to reduce unfairness; (3) capture per-pod sleep/wake metrics and check host kernel version and NTP events. Escalate to runtime lead if pulses persist after toggles.
